results.title: machine learning - Choosing the "Correct" Seed for Reproducible Research/Results - Cross Validated
results.content: The following day, I realized that I should have set a seed so that the random sample of indexes (rows) used to create the training and test sets are the same each time the code is run. I used a for loop 10,000 times, each time getting a new random sample of indices, created a new training and test set, built a linear model, predicted outcomes for the test set, and calculated the MSE. The last thing I did was loop through this same model building process until I found a seed that lead to an MSE in between the mean and the median of the 20,000 MSEs. The R code for this is:. for(i in 1:10000) { set.seed(i) index <- sample(x = 1:nrow(data), size = round(nrow(data)*0.75), replace = FALSE) train <- data[index, ] test <- data[-index, ] #Linear Model 1 - No Data Cleaning lm1.fit <- glm(medv ~ ., data = train) summary(lm1.fit) pr.lm1 <- predict(lm1.fit, test) error <- sum((pr.lm1 - test$medv)^2) / nrow(test) if(error > 23 & error < 24){print(i)} }. I believe that this method for obtaining a seed more accurately depicts a model's ability to accurately predict versus just randomly picking a seed or finding a seed which gives the best results (which I view as "cheating"). [Scortchi] Thanks - I was trying to be pithy & conflated two points: (1) Specifically the OP's re-inventing Monte-Carlo cross-validation; & (2) the sensitivity of the out-of-sample MSE estimate to the seed used shows that they should be using some form of re-sampling validation rather than a train/test split. First, when you select the seed based on the results, the simulation no longer is random. For another take on setting seeds see /questions/80407. * $\begingroup$ "The seed choice should not affect the ultimate result, otherwise you have an issue." For something like MCMC, this should be a reasonable assumption. The whole point of the seeds is that you've got a script that someone can use to completely reproduce the exact results you got. So you can use a seed to replicate exactly the results you saw...and then test how reliable that is by randomly using other seeds on the exact same script. If so many people use set.seed(123) doesn't that affect randomness of world's reporting?

You have a lot of hyperparameters, different dataset splits, different ways to preprocess your data, bugs, etc. Ideally, you should log data split (already preprocessed), all hyperparameters (including learning rate scheduling), the initial state of your model and optimizer, random seeds used for initialization, dataset shuffling and all of your code. 1. Track your model and optimizer hyperparameters (including learning rate schedule). 2. Save final model parameters. To save your hyperparameters you can use the TensorBoard HParams plugin, but we recommend using a specialized service like wandb.ai. These services not only store all of your logs but provide an easy interface to store hyperparameters, code and model files. 1. Save the exact code you used (create a tag in your repository for each run). 2. Save your preprocessed data, especially if you are working on a dataset paper (Data Version Control helps). 3. Save your model and optimizer initialization (the state at step 0). 4. Use GPU in deterministic mode (this will slightly affect the performance). # Before the training: import random import wandb import torch import numpy as np random seed args seed # python random generator np random seed args seed # numpy random generator torch manual_seed args seed torch cuda manual_seed_all args seed torch backends cudnn deterministic = True torch backends cudnn benchmark = False wandb init config = args # keep all your hyperparameters in args # wandb also saves your code files and git repository automatically checkpoint = 'model' model state_dict 'optimizer' optimizer state_dict 'settings' args 'epoch' epoch 'step' global_step torch save checkpoint save_path_for_init wandb save save_path_for_init # upload your initialization to wandb # Your training loop is here# After the training: checkpoint = 'model' model state_dict 'optimizer' optimizer state_dict 'settings' args 'epoch' epoch 'step' global_step torch save checkpoint save_path wandb save save_path # upload your trained model to wandb. * Fully reproducible research paper example.

results.title: Understanding and Using Random Seeds in Python - CodeRivers
results.content: The concept of a random seed is a fundamental aspect when dealing with random number generation. A random seed is a value that initializes a pseudorandom number generator. By setting a specific random seed, we can ensure reproducibility of seemingly random processes, which is essential for debugging, testing, and comparing results. 1. Fundamental Concepts of Random Seed in Python * Using `numpy` for numerical computing * Choosing the right seed value * When to set and not set a seed Fundamental Concepts of Random Seed in Python Python uses pseudorandom number generators. For example, if we have a simple random number generator that generates integers between 1 and 10, and we set the seed to 42, the first number it generates will always be the same. To set a random seed, we use the `random.seed()` function. # Set the random seed # Generate a random integer between 1 and 10 random_number = random.randint(1, 10) In this code, we first import the `random` module. # Set the random seed # Generate a random array of 5 numbers between 0 and 1 Here, we import `numpy` as `np`. We set the seed to 42 using `(42)` and then generate a random array of 5 numbers between 0 and 1 using `(5)`. # Set the random seeds # Your neural network code here In this example, we are using both `numpy` and `tensorflow`. By setting the seeds in both libraries, we can ensure that the random operations within the neural network, such as weight initialization, are reproducible. For example, when generating cryptographic keys, setting a seed would defeat the purpose of having a secure, random key. Random seeds in Python are a powerful tool for ensuring reproducibility in random number generation. Whether you are working on a small data analysis project or a large - scale machine learning experiment, understanding how to set and use random seeds correctly can save you a lot of time in debugging and validating results. * Python official documentation for the `random` module * `numpy` official documentation for random number generation * TensorFlow documentation on random seed setting DO NOT SELL OR SHARE MY INFORMATION

results.content: # Random seeds and reproducible results in PyTorch In this article, I will talk about random seeds and their effects and how to obtain reproducible results in PyTorch. >>> import torch>>> random_seed = 1>>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)>>> torch.rand(1,3)tensor()>>> torch.manual_seed(random_seed)>>> torch.rand(1,3)tensor() Here, we can see that the **initial weight values obtained depends on the state of the RNG,** which is why when I set the seed before every call to the init function, I can get the same initial weight values. Now that we have seen the effects of seed and the state of random number generator, we can look at how to obtain reproducible results in PyTorch. The following code snippet is a standard one that people use to obtain reproducible results in PyTorch.

results.title: PyTorch Training Checkpoint Exact Recovery Reproducibility - James D. McCaffreyJames D. McCaffrey
results.content: ## PyTorch Training Checkpoint Exact Recovery Reproducibility. About a year ago I spent many days figuring out how to save a PyTorch training checkpoint in such a way that it’s possible to load the saved information and resume training in a way that’s exactly like the original training. Briefly, I discovered that because there’s no way to save the state of a DataLoader object, you must manually reset the global PyTorch random number seed on each training epoch. Here’s the key code (with many details left out) to train a neural and save checkpoints so that training is exactly reproducible:. print("Starting training") net.train() for epoch in range(0, max_epochs): T.manual_seed(1 + epoch) # for recovery reproducibility epoch_loss = 0 # for one full epoch for (batch_idx, batch) in enumerate(train_ldr): X = batch['predictors'] # inputs Y = batch['targets'] # correct class/label/job optimizer.zero_grad() oupt = net(X) loss_val = loss_func(oupt, Y) # a tensor epoch_loss += loss_val.item() # accumulate loss_val.backward() optimizer.step() if epoch % ep_log_interval == 0: print("epoch = %4d loss = %0.4f" % (epoch, epoch_loss)) dt = time.strftime("%Y_%m_%d-%H_%M_%S") fn = ".\\Log\\" + str(dt) + str("-") + \ str(epoch) + "_checkpoint.pt" info_dict = { 'epoch' : epoch, 'numpy_random_state' : np.random.get_state(), 'torch_random_state' : T.random.get_rng_state(), 'net_state' : net.state_dict(), 'optimizer_state' : optimizer.state_dict() } T.save(info_dict, fn) print("Done training "). epoch_saved = chkpt['epoch'] + 1 for epoch in range(epoch_saved, max_epochs): T.manual_seed(1 + epoch) # for recovery reproducibility epoch_loss = 0 # for one full epoch for (batch_idx, batch) in enumerate(train_ldr): X = batch['predictors'] # inputs Y = batch['targets'] # correct class/label/job optimizer.zero_grad() oupt = net(X) loss_val = loss_func(oupt, Y) # a tensor epoch_loss += loss_val.item() # accumulate loss_val.backward() optimizer.step() if epoch % ep_log_interval == 0: print("epoch = %4d loss = %0.4f" % (epoch, epoch_loss)) dt = time.strftime("%Y_%m_%d-%H_%M_%S") fn = ".\\Log\\" + str(dt) + str("-") + \ str(epoch) + "_checkpoint.pt" info_dict = { 'epoch' : epoch, 'numpy_random_state' : np.random.get_state(), 'torch_random_state' : T.random.get_rng_state(), 'net_state' : net.state_dict(), 'optimizer_state' : optimizer.state_dict() } T.save(info_dict, fn) print("Done training "). If you don’t manually reset the PyTorch global seed on each epoch, when you reload a saved checkpoint, the resumed training will be close to, but not exactly the same as, the training that occurs without saving the checkpoint.
